description: Where space data meets human survival.
summary: ARES-1 is a web app that helps plan a safe walk on Mars, focused on Jezero Crater. It combines three kinds of real NASA orbital data: HiRISE terrain heights and images and CRISM mineral maps showing clay, olivine and carbonate signals. A global Mars view gives context. Users explore the terrain, pick a start point and a science target such as Kodiak butte, and ARES-1 plans a walking route that avoids steep slopes, craters and rough ground, checked at about 3 meters of detail. It then tests the route against spacesuit life-support figures from NASA’s Advanced EMU design paper and the emergency walk-back range, and gives a simple GO, CAUTION or NO-GO verdict. This address the Marswalk challenge by turning layered orbital data into a clear safety decision. On Mars, rescue is many months away, so astronauts need to know a route is safe before they leave. However, ARES-1 is a decision-support prototype, not flight-certified.
details:
What ARES-1 does?

ARES-1 helps space crews to plan a walking route and decide whether it is safe. It as 3 pages, Explore, Plan, and Assess.

  1. Explore: This shows real Jezero terrain with layers for steep slopes, rough ground and mineral signals. Users can click any point of the terrain to see its height, slope and minerals.
  2. Plan route: Users can choose a start and a target, such as Kodiak butte, or click on the map to plan the route.
  3. Assess: This page shows the full result: distance, time, life support used, and a GO, CAUTION or NO-GO verdict. Users can change the suit’s slope limit, walking pace and emergency window to see what changes.

How ARES-1 works?

Behind the scenes, ARES-1 calculates slope from NASA’s HiRISE terrain model and treats ground steeper than the suit limit (18° by default) as impassable. It then finds the shortest safe route with A*, a standard route-finding method, and avoids rough ground. It estimates walking time and life support for a round trip plus a science stop, using figures from NASA’s Advanced EMU design paper. Finally, it checks that the target is inside the emergency walk-back range, meaning how far a crew could walk home if the main life support failed. CRISM mineral maps are lined up with the HiRISE image, and areas with no mineral data are labelled as data gaps.

The benefits

Planners can see in one place where a crew can walk, where the science is, and whether the trip fits the suit’s limits. This helps crews preview a Marswalk before leaving the habitat and avoid unsafe routes. The same approach could be used at other sites that have HiRISE terrain data.

Tools & languages

  • Languages & Core Libraries: Python, NumPy, SciPy (Euclidean distance transforms and spatial filtering), Rasterio (GeoTIFF reprojection and grid alignment), Pillow.
  • Frontend & Visualization: Streamlit, Plotly (interactive 2D orbital maps, elevation profiles, and 3D Mars globe), HTML/CSS, and GeoJSON export.

What is creative about ARES-1?

ARES-1 joins terrain, imagery and mineral data with suit limits in one simple three-step flow. Its CAUTION verdict catches routes that pass the life-support check but go beyond the walk-back range. It is also honest about its limits and shows data gaps instead of hiding them.

Key factors considered

Safety came first. We measured and corrected a roughly 330 m offset between the CRISM and HiRISE maps. Besides, we kept the suit numbers adjustable and labelled the assumptions, such as the slope limit and walking pace.

On the other hand, we clearly state that orbital data cannot show boulders under about 3 m or loose sand, and that CRISM covers only part of the area. ARES-1 is a decision-support prototype and is not flight-certified.
